text: Why are lines of longitude called meridians?
options: Because all places along the same longitude experience local noon (midday) at the same instant
Because they form complete circles around the Earth, like latitudes
Because they measure distance in degrees from the Equator
Because they are used only to mark time zones on maps
explanation: The word 'meridian' comes from the Latin 'meridies' meaning midday; every place on a given longitude has the Sun overhead (local noon) at the same moment.

text: How many meridians of longitude lie to the east and to the west of the Prime Meridian respectively?
options: 90 and 90
360 and 0
explanation: The 360 degree circle around the Earth is divided equally by the Prime Meridian into 180 meridians running east and 180 running west, meeting at the 180th meridian (the approximate location of the International Date Line).

text: The Earth's axis is inclined at approximately _____ to the plane of its orbit around the Sun.
options: 45 degrees
90 degrees
23.5 degrees
66.5 degrees
explanation: The axis is tilted 23.5 degrees from the vertical (perpendicular to the orbital plane), which is the same as saying it is inclined at 66.5 degrees to the plane of the orbit itself.

text: The uniform time followed throughout a country or region, based on a single central meridian, is called:
options: Standard Time
Local Time
Greenwich Mean Time
Universal Time
explanation: Standard Time is the uniform time adopted by a country based on one chosen central meridian, so that all places within it share the same clock time regardless of their individual local time.

text: Why is the Equator considered the longest line of latitude?
options: Because it divides the Earth into two unequal hemispheres
Because it is a Great Circle passing through the Earth's centre, giving it the largest circumference of all parallels
Because all meridians of longitude converge at the Equator
Because it is numbered 0 degrees
explanation: The Equator is the only parallel of latitude whose plane passes through the centre of the Earth, making it a Great Circle with the maximum possible circumference; all other parallels are smaller circles.

text: Why does local time vary from place to place on the Earth?
options: Because all places face the Sun at exactly the same moment
Because the Earth rotates from west to east, so places to the east face the Sun earlier than places to the west
Because the Sun rises at a single fixed universal moment everywhere
Because longitude has no real effect on time
explanation: As the Earth rotates west to east, the Sun appears to rise earlier for places farther east; since local time is based on the position of the Sun overhead, it differs by 4 minutes for every degree of longitude.

text: What is the significance of the Tropic of Cancer (23.5 degrees N)?
options: It is the line of 0 degrees latitude
It marks the beginning of the Arctic Circle
It is the northernmost latitude at which the midday Sun can be directly overhead
It is the latitude that receives the least rainfall on Earth
explanation: The Tropic of Cancer marks the northernmost point reached by the Sun's vertical rays, occurring at the Summer Solstice (around 21 June); beyond this latitude the midday Sun is never directly overhead.

text: Why does the International Date Line (IDL) follow a zigzag path instead of running perfectly straight along 180 degrees?
options: To align exactly with the Equator
To mark the exact location of the Prime Meridian
To separate the hot and cold climatic zones of the Earth
To avoid cutting through land areas and island groups, so that neighbouring places are not split into two different calendar dates
explanation: The IDL is deliberately bent at several points so that it passes through open ocean rather than through inhabited land or island nations, avoiding the confusion of having two different dates within the same country.

text: What is meant by the Winter Solstice (in the Northern Hemisphere)?
options: The day when day and night are exactly equal everywhere on Earth
The day, around 22 December, when the Sun's vertical rays fall on the Tropic of Capricorn, giving the Northern Hemisphere its shortest day and longest night
The day the Southern Hemisphere experiences its shortest night of the year
The day when the Sun is directly overhead the Equator
explanation: At the Winter Solstice the Earth's tilt points the Northern Hemisphere away from the Sun, so the Sun appears overhead the Tropic of Capricorn, giving the Northern Hemisphere its shortest day and the Southern Hemisphere its longest day.

text: Which latitude is referred to as the 'Land of the Midnight Sun', and why?
options: The Arctic Circle (66.5 degrees N), because during its summer the Sun remains visible there even at midnight
The Tropic of Cancer, because of its long summer days
The Antarctic Circle, because of the Aurora lights visible at night
The Equator, because the Sun is overhead there throughout the year
explanation: Within the Arctic Circle, the axial tilt causes continuous daylight for part of the summer, so the Sun stays above the horizon even at midnight; hence the name 'Land of the Midnight Sun'.

text: Why does Kuala Lumpur (near the Equator) rotate faster on the Earth's axis than a city like London?
options: Because places near the Equator trace out a much larger circle in one rotation, so their linear rotational speed is greater than at higher latitudes
Because Kuala Lumpur is at a higher altitude than London
Because Kuala Lumpur receives more sunlight than London
Because Kuala Lumpur is in a different time zone from London
explanation: The Earth's circumference is largest at the Equator and decreases towards the poles; since every point completes one rotation in 24 hours, places closer to the Equator must travel a greater linear distance, i.e. move faster.

text: Why do certain years have 366 days instead of the usual 365 (leap years)?
options: Because of a shift in the position of the Prime Meridian
Because of the occurrence of an equinox that year
Because the Earth actually takes about 365 and a quarter days to revolve around the Sun, and the extra quarter-day is added as one whole day every fourth year
Because the Moon's orbit occasionally adds an extra day to the calendar
explanation: One revolution of the Earth around the Sun actually takes about 365 days 5 hours 48 minutes; the leftover time accumulates to roughly one full day every four years, which is added as 29 February in a leap year.

text: What is a Great Circle, and which parallel of latitude is itself a Great Circle?
options: A circle on the globe whose plane passes through the Earth's centre and divides it into two equal halves; among all latitudes, only the Equator is a Great Circle
The Tropic of Cancer, because it is used for navigation
The Arctic Circle, because it marks the polar day/night zone
Any large circle that can be drawn on a world map
explanation: A Great Circle's plane must pass through the centre of the sphere, dividing it into two equal hemispheres; of all the latitude circles, only the Equator satisfies this, since all other parallels are smaller circles offset from the centre.

text: Why do aircraft generally follow Great Circle routes on long-distance flights?
options: Because the arc of a Great Circle gives the shortest possible distance between two points on the Earth's curved surface
Because Great Circle routes always run along the Equator
Because Great Circle routes always avoid bad weather
Because international law requires all flights to follow the Equator
explanation: On a sphere, the shortest path between two points lies along the arc of the Great Circle joining them, so pilots use Great Circle routes to save flying distance, time and fuel.

text: Which of the following is valid evidence that the Earth is spherical in shape?
options: The presence of gravity on Earth
The changing of seasons through the year
A ship sailing away from an observer disappears hull-first over the horizon, with the mast visible last
The occurrence of day and night
explanation: As a ship sails away on a curved (spherical) surface, its lower hull dips below the horizon first while the mast remains visible longest — this could not happen on a flat surface, and is classic evidence of Earth's curvature.

text: Which of the following is evidence that the Earth is a geoid (a sphere slightly flattened at the poles) rather than a perfect sphere?
options: The Earth has a magnetic field
The Earth revolves around the Sun once a year
The Earth's polar diameter is about 43 km less than its equatorial diameter, due to the flattening caused by its rotation
The Earth has oceans covering most of its surface
explanation: The centrifugal effect of the Earth's rotation causes a slight bulge at the Equator and flattening at the poles, so the equatorial diameter (about 12,756 km) is larger than the polar diameter (about 12,714 km) by roughly 43 km.

text: Which of the following is a direct effect of the Earth's rotation (spinning on its axis), rather than its revolution around the Sun?
options: The occurrence of day and night
The variation of climate with latitude
The occurrence of a leap year
The occurrence of the four seasons
explanation: Rotation on its axis makes different parts of the Earth face or turn away from the Sun every 24 hours, causing day and night; seasons, climatic variation with latitude, and leap years are all related instead to the Earth's revolution and its axial tilt.

text: Why does Indian Standard Time (IST), based on a single standard meridian, help in organising a uniform schedule for transport like railways and airways?
options: Because IST is based on the Equator rather than a meridian
Because IST changes automatically with the seasons
Because it gives every part of the country the same clock time, avoiding the confusion that would result if each place used its own local time
Because IST is identical to Greenwich Mean Time
explanation: India's local time would otherwise vary from place to place because of its longitudinal spread; by adopting one Standard Time (based on 82.5 degrees E), timetables for trains and flights across the country can be coordinated on a single, shared clock.

text: What is the Barosphere?
options: The floor of the ocean
The lowest layer of the atmosphere
The outermost solid layer of the Earth's surface only
Another name for the Earth's solid interior, made up of concentric layers of increasing density towards the centre
explanation: Barosphere is a term for the Earth's interior as a whole, consisting of the crust, mantle and core, with density increasing progressively towards the centre.

text: Which statement correctly compares the Earth's mantle and crust?
options: The crust and mantle have the same thickness
The crust is thicker than the mantle
The crust is denser than the mantle
The mantle is far thicker (about 2,900 km) and denser than the thin, comparatively light crust
explanation: The crust is only 5 to 70 km thick, while the mantle extends to a depth of about 2,900 km and is made of denser silicate rock than the crust above it.

text: Which of the following correctly represents the order of the Earth's layers from the surface downward, by composition?
options: SIAL - NIFE - SIMA
NIFE - SIAL - SIMA
NIFE - SIMA - SIAL
SIAL - SIMA - NIFE
explanation: The outer crust is divided into an upper SIAL layer (silica-aluminium rich, e.g. granite) and a lower SIMA layer (silica-magnesium rich, e.g. basalt); below these lies the NIFE layer of the core, rich in nickel and iron.

text: The Moho (Mohorovicic) discontinuity, which marks the boundary between the crust and mantle, lies at approximately:
options: 8 km beneath the oceans and 32 km beneath the continents
8 km beneath the oceans and 30 km beneath the continents
8 km beneath the oceans and 31 km beneath the continents
10 km beneath the oceans and 32 km beneath the continents
explanation: The crust is much thinner under the oceans (around 5-10 km) than under the continents (around 30-40 km); textbook figures commonly used are about 8 km oceanic and 32 km continental depth for the Moho discontinuity.

text: Name an element that is found abundantly in both the Earth's crust and the Earth's core.
options: Nitrogen
Chlorine
Helium
Iron
explanation: Iron is a major component of crustal rocks and minerals, and it is also the dominant metal (along with nickel) that makes up the Earth's core, which is why it is referred to as the NIFE layer.

text: Why does the inner core of the Earth remain solid despite its extremely high temperature?
options: Because the inner core does not receive any heat
Because the enormous pressure exerted by all the overlying layers keeps the iron-nickel material in a solid state
Because the inner core is made of rock, not metal
Because the inner core is actually cooler than the outer core
explanation: Although the inner core's temperature is very high (over 5000 degrees C), the immense pressure from the weight of all the overlying layers prevents the iron-nickel alloy from melting, keeping it solid, unlike the molten (liquid) outer core.

text: Which layer of the Earth is primarily responsible for the Earth's magnetism?
options: The mantle
The core (particularly the molten, iron-nickel outer core)
The crust
The atmosphere
explanation: Convective movements of molten iron and nickel in the outer core generate electric currents that produce the Earth's magnetic field, a phenomenon known as the geodynamo effect.

text: What is the contact zone between the Earth's mantle and its core called?
options: The Conrad discontinuity
The Moho discontinuity
The Lehmann discontinuity
The Gutenberg discontinuity
explanation: The Gutenberg discontinuity, found at a depth of about 2,900 km, marks the boundary where the solid mantle gives way to the molten outer core.

text: The layer of the Earth that makes up most of its total mass and volume is the:
options: Crust
Mantle
Atmosphere
Core
explanation: The mantle, extending from the base of the crust to a depth of about 2,900 km, accounts for roughly 84% of the Earth's total volume and about two-thirds of its mass, making it the largest of the Earth's layers.

text: The layer of the Earth's interior that lies directly below the lithosphere is the:
options: Sima
Asthenosphere
Mesosphere
Barysphere
explanation: The asthenosphere is the partly molten, plastic layer of the upper mantle lying just below the rigid lithosphere; its weak, flowing rock allows tectonic plates above to move.

text: Why does the temperature rise gradually as we move towards the interior of the Earth?
options: Because the interior contains large deposits of ice that release heat
Because of residual heat left over from the Earth's formation and continuous heat released by the decay of radioactive elements deep inside
Because the Sun's heat penetrates and accumulates through the crust
Because of friction generated by ocean currents at the surface
explanation: The geothermal gradient (increase of temperature with depth) is mainly caused by heat retained since the Earth's formation and ongoing heat generated by the radioactive decay of elements such as uranium and thorium within the mantle and core.

text: Which type of rock is crystalline in nature?
options: None of these
Igneous rock
Sedimentary rock
All rocks equally
explanation: Igneous rocks form from the cooling and solidification of molten magma or lava, a process that allows mineral grains to arrange into a crystalline structure.

text: How are foliated (banded) metamorphic rocks, such as gneiss, typically formed?
options: By the realignment of mineral grains into parallel bands under intense directional heat and pressure
By limestone being dissolved in rainwater
By the rapid cooling of lava at the Earth's surface
By the simple deposition of sediment layers on a riverbed
explanation: Foliation occurs when platy or elongated minerals in a rock are reoriented into parallel layers or bands under strong directional pressure and heat during metamorphism, producing a banded texture seen in rocks like gneiss and schist.

text: What are fossils, and in which type of rock are they typically found?
options: Fossils are found equally in all rock types
Fossils are the preserved remains or traces of ancient plants and animals, found mainly in sedimentary rocks
Fossils are mineral veins found mainly in metamorphic rocks
Fossils are crystals found mainly in igneous rocks
explanation: Sedimentary rocks form in layers through the gradual deposition and compaction of sediment, which can trap and preserve the remains of organisms as fossils; igneous and metamorphic rocks involve heat and pressure that destroy such remains.

text: Why are sedimentary rocks generally more prone to erosion than igneous rocks?
options: Because sedimentary rocks are usually softer, less compact and often more porous than the hard, tightly crystalline igneous rocks
Because sedimentary rocks are always located underwater
Because igneous rocks dissolve easily in water
Because sedimentary rocks are always found only in deserts
explanation: The loosely cemented, layered structure of many sedimentary rocks makes them softer and more porous than the dense, interlocking crystalline structure of igneous rocks, so they wear away faster under weathering and erosion.

text: Why does a batholith often form the core of major mountain systems?
options: Because batholiths are sedimentary rocks formed by river deposition
Because it is a huge, dome-shaped mass of intrusive igneous rock that solidifies deep underground and becomes exposed as softer overlying rock is gradually eroded away
Because batholiths are always found along coastlines
Because batholiths are formed only by wind erosion
explanation: A batholith is an enormous body of cooled magma that solidifies far below the surface; over geological time, the softer rock layers above it erode away, exposing the resistant batholith as the hard core of a mountain range.

text: Why are carbonaceous sedimentary rocks, such as coal, of great importance to industry?
options: Because they are used only as decorative building stone
Because they are a primary source of precious metals like gold
Because they are formed from compressed and altered plant matter and serve as a major source of fuel and energy
Because they form the Earth's core
explanation: Carbonaceous rocks like coal are the organic remains of ancient vegetation, compressed and altered over millions of years; they are burned as a fuel and are a key raw material for the energy and steel industries.

text: Why does the size of mineral crystals in igneous rocks vary from very small to very large?
options: Because of the amount of water mixed with the rock
Because of how old the rock is
Because of the amount of wind erosion the rock has experienced
Because the rate at which magma or lava cools differs — slow cooling deep underground allows large crystals to form, while rapid cooling at the surface forms small crystals
explanation: Crystal size in igneous rocks depends on cooling rate: magma trapped deep underground cools slowly, giving minerals time to grow into large crystals (as in granite), while lava erupted at the surface cools quickly, producing fine or no crystals (as in basalt or obsidian).

text: Shale is an example of a:
options: Sedimentary rock
Mineral
Metamorphic rock
Igneous rock
explanation: Shale is a fine-grained sedimentary rock formed by the compaction of clay and silt particles deposited in layers.

text: Gneiss is an example of a:
options: Metamorphic rock
Igneous rock
Mineral
Sedimentary rock
explanation: Gneiss is a banded (foliated) metamorphic rock formed when existing rocks are subjected to intense heat and pressure deep within the Earth.

text: What is the metamorphosed form of Shale, and of Limestone, respectively?
options: Gneiss and Quartzite
Slate and Marble
Marble and Slate
Quartzite and Gneiss
explanation: Under heat and pressure, shale (a clay-rich sedimentary rock) metamorphoses into slate, while limestone (a calcareous sedimentary rock) metamorphoses into marble.

text: Why are igneous rocks also known as 'primary rocks'?
options: Because they are found only at very high altitudes
Because they were the first rocks to form on Earth, solidifying directly from cooling magma, with all other rock types ultimately derived from them
Because they are the most common rock type visible on the surface today
Because they always contain fossils
explanation: Igneous rocks form directly from the cooling and solidifying of molten material and are considered the original, 'parent' rocks from which sedimentary rocks (through weathering and deposition) and metamorphic rocks (through heat and pressure) are eventually derived.

text: What is the key difference between a Rock and a Mineral?
options: A rock and a mineral are exactly the same thing
A rock is a naturally occurring aggregate of one or more minerals, while a mineral is a naturally occurring inorganic substance with a fixed, definite chemical composition
A rock is always harder than any mineral
A mineral is always larger in size than a rock
explanation: Minerals are the basic chemical building blocks with a specific composition and crystal structure (e.g. quartz, feldspar, mica), while rocks are naturally occurring masses made up of one or more such minerals combined together.

text: How do Plutonic rocks differ from Hypabyssal rocks?
options: There is no real difference between the two
Plutonic rocks solidify very slowly deep within the Earth, forming large crystals, while hypabyssal rocks solidify faster at intermediate depths, forming medium-sized crystals
Hypabyssal rocks are always sedimentary in origin
Plutonic rocks are extrusive while hypabyssal rocks are intrusive
explanation: Both are intrusive igneous rocks, but plutonic rocks (e.g. granite) solidify at great depth and cool extremely slowly, producing large crystals, while hypabyssal rocks (e.g. dolerite) solidify closer to the surface and cool faster, producing smaller crystals.

text: How do Extrusive and Intrusive igneous rocks differ from one another?
options: Extrusive rocks form on the Earth's surface from rapidly cooling lava and are fine-grained, while intrusive rocks solidify below the surface from slowly cooling magma and are coarse-grained
Extrusive rocks are always sedimentary in nature
There is no textural difference between the two types
Intrusive rocks always contain fossils
explanation: Lava that erupts and cools quickly at the surface forms fine-grained extrusive rocks (e.g. basalt), whereas magma that solidifies slowly beneath the surface forms coarse-grained intrusive rocks (e.g. granite).

text: Fold mountains, such as the Himalayas, are formed mainly by:
options: The folding of rock layers due to strong compressional forces when tectonic plates collide
Volcanic eruption alone, with no plate movement involved
The deposition of wind-blown sand over long periods
The faulting and vertical uplift of large rock blocks
explanation: When two tectonic plates collide, the immense compressional force buckles and folds the sedimentary rock layers between them upward into fold mountains, as seen in the formation of the Himalayas.

text: Block mountains are formed mainly through the process of:
options: The gradual accumulation of volcanic lava
Faulting, where a block of land is thrust upward or the surrounding land subsides, leaving the block standing above its surroundings
Wind erosion of softer surrounding rock
The folding of rock strata under compression
explanation: Block mountains (e.g. the Vosges and Black Forest in Europe) form when faulting causes a section of the crust to be uplifted relative to the surrounding land, or when the land on either side subsides, leaving a raised block.

text: Why are certain old, eroded mountains, such as the Aravalli Range, called 'mountains of denudation' or relict mountains?
options: Because they are the youngest mountain ranges on Earth
Because they were formed instantly by a single large earthquake
Because they were once much higher, but have been gradually worn down by long-term weathering and erosion, leaving low, rounded remnants
Because they are entirely artificial, man-made structures
explanation: Mountains of denudation are the remains of once-lofty mountain ranges that have been worn down over millions of years by continuous weathering and erosion, leaving behind low, rounded hills such as the Aravallis.

text: Orogenesis refers to the process of formation of:
options: Valleys
Plateaus
Mountains
Deltas
explanation: Orogenesis is the geological term for the process of mountain building, typically resulting from the folding, faulting or volcanic activity associated with tectonic plate movement.

text: An intermountain (intermontane) plateau is one that is:
options: Formed entirely by river delta deposits
Found only on the ocean floor
Formed entirely of volcanic ash with no rock base
Surrounded on all sides by high mountain ranges
explanation: An intermountain plateau, such as the Tibetan Plateau, lies enclosed by high mountain ranges on all sides, distinguishing it from plateaus found at the edge of a continent or between a mountain range and the sea.

text: Why are plateaus considered to be of great economic importance to human beings?
options: Because they have no economic significance at all
Because they are often rich in minerals and provide excellent sites for hydroelectric power generation due to their steep river-cut edges
Because they always have the most fertile soil of any landform
Because they are always located along the coast
explanation: Many plateaus, such as the Chotanagpur Plateau in India, are storehouses of valuable minerals, and rivers descending from their steep edges can be harnessed to generate hydroelectric power.

text: Why are plateaus also referred to as 'tablelands'?
options: Because they are the flattest landform found anywhere on Earth
Because they have a relatively flat top with comparatively steep sides, resembling the surface of a table
Because they are always perfectly square in shape
Because they are used mainly to grow crops on raised tables
explanation: A plateau is an elevated area of land with a broad, flat or gently undulating top and steep sides descending to the surrounding lowland, similar in profile to a table — hence the name 'tableland'.

text: Depositional plains are formed mainly by:
options: The folding of the Earth's crust under compression
The deposition of sediments carried by rivers, wind, glaciers or ocean waves
Sudden, violent volcanic explosions
The faulting and vertical displacement of rock layers
explanation: Unlike structural plains (formed by the upliftment of land) or erosional plains (formed by wearing away of land), depositional plains are built up from material deposited by rivers, wind, ice or the sea.

text: Why are river floodplains (alluvial plains) often regarded as the 'granaries of the world'?
options: Because they are always found in cold climates unsuitable for other crops
Because floods deposit fine, mineral-rich silt over them, making the soil exceptionally fertile and ideal for farming
Because they consist mainly of hard, infertile rock
Because they are completely free from the risk of flooding
explanation: Each time a river floods, it leaves behind a fresh layer of fine, nutrient-rich alluvial silt on the surrounding plain, continually renewing the soil's fertility and making floodplains some of the most productive farmland in the world.

text: What are Structural plains?
options: Plains formed entirely by the deposition of wind-blown sand
Plains formed by the upliftment of a section of the sea floor above sea level, with the original rock layers largely undisturbed
Plains formed by the slow erosion of a mountain range
Plains formed by sudden volcanic eruption
explanation: Structural plains originate when a part of the ocean floor is gently uplifted above sea level by crustal movements, without much folding or disturbance, so the rock strata remain largely in their original, horizontal arrangement.

text: What is 'Bhabhar', and where is this region found in India?
options: A coastal plain found along the Gujarat coastline
A narrow belt of porous, pebbly deposits at the foot of the Himalayas, where many streams disappear underground
A desert region found in western Rajasthan
A fertile alluvial plain found in the middle Ganga basin
explanation: The Bhabhar is a narrow belt running along the foothills of the Himalayas, made up of coarse, porous pebbles and gravel deposited by Himalayan rivers; because the material is so porous, many smaller streams sink into the ground and disappear here.

text: What is the technical term for the peeling off of the outer layers of a rock due to repeated expansion and contraction caused by temperature change?
options: Block disintegration
Exfoliation
Hydration
Carbonation
explanation: Exfoliation occurs when a rock's outer surface heats up and expands faster than its cooler interior during the day, and contracts faster at night, causing successive outer shells to peel away like the layers of an onion.

text: Which type of chemical weathering is responsible for the formation of stalactites and stalagmites in limestone caves?
options: Exfoliation
Oxidation
Hydration
Carbonation
explanation: Carbonation occurs when rainwater containing dissolved carbon dioxide forms a weak carbonic acid that dissolves limestone; as this mineral-rich water drips and evaporates inside caves, it redeposits calcium carbonate, building up stalactites (hanging) and stalagmites (rising from the floor).

text: What is Frost Action (the freeze-thaw process) in weathering?
options: The repeated freezing and thawing of water trapped in rock cracks, which expands and gradually widens the cracks until the rock breaks apart
The dissolving of limestone by slightly acidic rainwater
The slow growth of plant roots into rock crevices
The oxidation of iron-bearing minerals within a rock
explanation: Water that seeps into cracks in a rock expands by about 9% when it freezes into ice, exerting great pressure on the surrounding rock; repeated freezing and thawing progressively widens the crack until the rock splits, a process common in cold and temperate regions.

text: How are human beings responsible for accelerating the weathering of rocks?
options: Through activities such as mining, quarrying, deforestation and construction, which expose rock surfaces to the elements and speed up their breakdown
By controlling the amount of rainfall a region receives
Human activity has no effect on the weathering of rock
By directly triggering earthquakes that break rocks apart
explanation: Human activities like quarrying, mining, clearing forests and building roads strip away the protective soil and vegetation cover, exposing bare rock directly to temperature changes, rainfall and wind, thereby accelerating natural weathering.

text: How does the common rock-forming mineral feldspar assist the process of hydration?
options: Feldspar chemically reacts with water, absorbing it and converting into soft clay minerals, which causes the rock containing it to swell, weaken and crumble
Feldspar repels all water and therefore prevents hydration from occurring
Feldspar reacts only with oxygen gas, never with water
Feldspar dissolves completely and instantly on contact with rainwater
explanation: Feldspar, a common mineral in rocks like granite, absorbs water molecules into its crystal structure and is chemically altered into clay minerals (such as kaolin); this absorption causes the mineral to expand, weakening the rock and causing it to disintegrate.

text: What is Oxidation, in the context of chemical weathering of rocks?
options: The dissolving of limestone by acidic water
The physical breaking of rock purely due to temperature change
The growth of ice crystals within rock cracks
The chemical reaction of oxygen (usually combined with moisture) with minerals, especially iron, in a rock, which causes it to 'rust' and crumble
explanation: Oxidation occurs when oxygen in the air or in water reacts with iron-bearing minerals in a rock, forming iron oxide (rust); this weakens the rock's structure, causing it to become brittle, discoloured (reddish-brown) and crumble.

text: What is Hydration, as a process of chemical weathering?
options: The complete drying out of a rock in desert conditions
The chemical combination of carbon with a mineral
The mechanical splitting of rock due to repeated frost action
The chemical process by which certain minerals in a rock absorb water and expand, weakening and breaking apart the rock
explanation: In hydration, minerals such as feldspar or anhydrite absorb water molecules into their structure and increase in volume; this expansion creates internal stress that weakens and eventually breaks apart the surrounding rock.

text: Why are rocks containing dark-coloured minerals generally more prone to physical (mechanical) weathering by temperature change?
options: Because dark minerals are always softer than light-coloured minerals
Because dark minerals absorb more heat from sunlight, causing greater expansion by day and contraction by night, which stresses and cracks the rock
Because dark minerals attract a greater amount of rainfall
Because dark minerals are naturally magnetic and attract lightning
explanation: Dark-coloured minerals absorb more solar radiation than light-coloured ones, so rocks containing them heat up more during the day and cool more at night; this larger daily temperature range causes greater expansion and contraction, promoting cracking.

text: Why are wells in desert regions often brackish (salty) in taste?
options: Because desert rock is always pure limestone
Because desert wells are usually connected underground to the sea
Because the very high rate of evaporation in deserts concentrates the dissolved salts present in the limited groundwater
Because deserts receive abundant fresh rainfall that dilutes the salt
explanation: With little rainfall to replenish groundwater and very high evaporation rates, the small amount of water present in desert aquifers becomes increasingly concentrated with dissolved mineral salts over time, making it taste brackish.

text: Why does vegetation cover generally help to reduce mechanical weathering and erosion of rock surfaces?
options: Because plants absorb all rainfall completely, so no water ever reaches the rock
Because plant roots and foliage shield the rock from extreme temperature changes and bind loose soil and rock particles together
Vegetation actually has no real effect on the weathering of rock
Because plant roots chemically dissolve the rock they grow on
explanation: A cover of vegetation shades rock surfaces from direct sun and wind, moderating temperature swings, while root systems help bind soil and loose rock fragments in place, both of which slow down the rate of weathering and erosion.

text: What is the technical term for weathering caused by the activities of plants, animals and microorganisms?
options: Chemical weathering
Biological (organic) weathering
Glacial weathering
Mechanical weathering
explanation: Biological weathering refers to the breakdown of rock caused by living organisms — for example, plant roots growing into cracks and widening them, or burrowing animals and lichen chemically altering rock surfaces.

text: Which of the following is a CONSTRUCTIVE effect of weathering?
options: It always triggers earthquakes
It helps break down parent rock into the fine particles that form fertile soil
It causes a permanent rise in sea level
It instantly converts solid rock into molten lava
explanation: While weathering can destructively wear away rock and landforms, it also plays a vital constructive role by breaking down rock into the smaller mineral particles that, mixed with organic matter, eventually form soil suitable for plant growth.

text: What is a Seismograph used for?
options: To measure wind speed
To measure atmospheric pressure
To record and measure the vibrations (seismic waves) produced by an earthquake
To measure rainfall
explanation: A seismograph is an instrument that detects and records the ground vibrations caused by seismic waves travelling through the Earth during an earthquake, producing a trace called a seismogram.

text: What is Volcanicity?
options: The process of mountain building through folding
The process of soil erosion by wind
The process by which molten magma, gases and other materials are forced out from the Earth's interior onto the surface
The process of glacier formation
explanation: Volcanicity (or vulcanicity) refers to all the processes associated with the movement of molten rock, gases and fragmented material from within the Earth to its surface, including volcanic eruptions and the formation of intrusive and extrusive features.

text: Which of the following is an example of an anthropogenic (human-caused) factor that can trigger an earthquake?
options: The movement of tectonic plates
Underground nuclear weapons testing or the filling of large reservoirs behind dams
A meteor striking the Earth
A volcanic eruption
explanation: While most earthquakes are caused by natural tectonic movement, human activities such as underground nuclear explosions, deep mining, and the immense added weight of water in large dam reservoirs can also induce or trigger seismic activity.

text: The Richter scale is used to measure the:
options: Intensity of a volcanic eruption
Atmospheric pressure
Speed of wind
Magnitude (energy released) of an earthquake
explanation: The Richter scale is a logarithmic scale that measures the magnitude of an earthquake, based on the amount of energy released at its source, as recorded by seismographs.

text: The Modified Mercalli scale grades earthquakes based on:
options: The depth of the earthquake's focus below the surface
The distance of a location from the epicentre
The exact energy released at the earthquake's source
Observed effects and damage, on a 12-point scale
explanation: Unlike the Richter scale (which measures energy released), the Modified Mercalli scale classifies earthquakes from I to XII based on their observed effects on people, buildings and the landscape at a given location.

text: The Epicentre of an earthquake is:
options: The point farthest away from the earthquake's effects
The specific location of a seismograph station
The exact underground point where the earthquake originates
The point on the Earth's surface located directly above the underground origin of the earthquake, where shaking is usually most intense
explanation: The focus is the underground point of origin, while the epicentre is the point on the surface directly above it; because it is closest to the source, the epicentre generally experiences the strongest tremors and the most damage.

text: The Focus of an earthquake is:
options: A safe zone identified during an earthquake
The instrument used to record seismic waves
The point on the surface directly above the earthquake's origin
The point within the Earth's crust where the earthquake actually originates
explanation: The focus (or hypocentre) is the exact underground location where rock first ruptures and seismic waves originate; the epicentre is simply its projection onto the Earth's surface.

text: Which type of seismic wave is unable to travel through liquids, such as the Earth's molten outer core?
options: Secondary (S) waves
All seismic waves travel equally well through liquids
Primary (P) waves
Surface (L) waves
explanation: Secondary (S) waves are shear waves that can only travel through solid material, so they cannot pass through the liquid outer core; this behaviour is one of the key indirect evidences used to determine that the outer core is molten.

text: Why are Primary (P) waves the first earthquake waves to be recorded on a seismogram?
options: Because they are the slowest waves but recorded first by convention
Because they are the fastest-travelling type of seismic wave and can pass through both solids and liquids
Because they always originate exactly at the surface
Because they travel only through the crust and never deeper
explanation: P waves are compressional waves that travel faster than all other seismic wave types and can move through both solid and liquid material, so they are always the first to arrive at a recording station after an earthquake.

text: Why is the Himalayan region of India especially prone to frequent earthquakes?
options: Because of deforestation in the region alone
Because it lies in a zone of active tectonic collision, where the Indian Plate is continuously pushing into the Eurasian Plate, as part of a young, seismically active fold mountain belt
Because it receives the highest rainfall in India
Because it lies far from any tectonic plate boundary
explanation: The Himalayas were formed, and continue to rise, because of the ongoing collision between the Indian and Eurasian tectonic plates; this active plate boundary makes the region highly prone to frequent earthquakes.

text: Japan experiences frequent earthquakes mainly because it is located in:
options: The Mid-Atlantic Ridge zone
A stable continental interior, far from any plate boundary
The Circum-Pacific Belt ('Ring of Fire')
A region directly on the Equator
explanation: Japan lies along the Circum-Pacific Belt, popularly called the 'Ring of Fire', where the Pacific Plate interacts with several surrounding plates, making it one of the most seismically and volcanically active regions in the world.

text: Why are earthquakes and volcanic activity both common in regions of young fold mountains?
options: Because fold mountains have no real connection to tectonic plate movement
Because these regions always receive the highest rainfall in the world
Because young mountains are always made of the softest possible rock
Because young fold mountains lie along active tectonic plate boundaries, where ongoing plate movement generates both volcanic eruptions and seismic activity
explanation: Young fold mountains, such as the Andes and the Himalayas, form at active plate boundaries where plates are still colliding or subducting; this same plate activity also generates volcanic eruptions and frequent earthquakes in these regions.

text: Arthur's Seat, in Edinburgh, is an example of a/an:
options: Active volcano
Shield volcano currently erupting
Dormant volcano
Extinct volcano
explanation: Arthur's Seat is the remnant of a volcano that was active around 350 million years ago and shows no sign of ever erupting again, making it a classic example of an extinct volcano.

text: Mount Vesuvius in Italy, which remained inactive for a long period before erupting violently in 79 A.D. and has erupted periodically since, is an example of a/an:
options: Dormant volcano
Extinct volcano
Shield volcano only
Active volcano erupting continuously
explanation: A dormant (sleeping) volcano is one that is not currently erupting but has erupted within recorded history and retains the potential to erupt again; Vesuvius, inactive for centuries before its famous 79 A.D. eruption that buried Pompeii, exemplifies this.

text: Which famous dormant volcano in Tanzania, Africa, is often described as a 'sleeping volcano'?
options: Mount Fuji
Mount Vesuvius
Mount Kilimanjaro
Mount Etna
explanation: Mount Kilimanjaro, Africa's highest peak, is a dormant stratovolcano; it last erupted thousands of years ago but is not classified as extinct, since it could potentially become active again in the future.

text: Why are dormant volcanoes sometimes called 'sleeping volcanoes'?
options: Because they are completely extinct and have no magma chamber left
Because they are not currently erupting but still retain the potential to become active again in the future
Because they only occur in very cold climates
Because they will never erupt again under any circumstances
explanation: A dormant volcano is in an inactive phase, showing no current signs of eruption, yet it is not considered permanently extinct because geological evidence suggests it still has the potential to erupt again.

text: The bowl or funnel-shaped depression formed at the mouth of a volcanic vent is called the:
options: Crater
Ash cloud
Magma chamber
Caldera plug
explanation: The crater is the bowl-shaped opening at the summit of a volcano, through which lava, ash and gases are ejected during an eruption; it forms directly around the vent.

text: The Magma Chamber of a volcano is:
options: The crater found at the volcano's summit
The vent through which lava flows out onto the surface
The underground reservoir where molten rock (magma) accumulates before being erupted
The cone of ash that builds up around the vent
explanation: The magma chamber is a large pool of molten rock within the Earth's crust that feeds a volcano; pressure build-up within this chamber eventually forces magma up through the vent during an eruption.

text: A Dyke is an intrusive volcanic feature formed when magma:
options: Forms the deep, irregular core of a mountain range (a batholith)
Solidifies within a vertical, sheet-like crack that cuts across existing rock layers
Forms a dome-shaped mass that arches the overlying rock layers (a laccolith)
Solidifies in a horizontal sheet running parallel to existing rock layers (a sill)
explanation: A dyke is a wall-like body of igneous rock that forms when magma is forced into and solidifies within a near-vertical fracture that cuts across the surrounding (often horizontal) rock strata.

text: Volcanic eruptions are closely associated with the theory of plate tectonics because:
options: Plate tectonics explains only earthquakes and has no connection to volcanic activity
Volcanoes form only at the exact centre of continents, away from any plate edge
Volcanoes occur completely at random, with no relationship to plate movement
Most volcanoes occur along plate boundaries, where the collision, separation or subduction of tectonic plates allows magma to rise to the surface
explanation: The majority of the world's active volcanoes are concentrated along tectonic plate boundaries (such as the Circum-Pacific Belt), where plate collision or divergence creates pathways for magma from the mantle to reach the surface.

text: What is an Ox-bow lake, and how is it formed?
options: A lake formed by glacial erosion in a mountain valley
A horseshoe-shaped lake formed when a meandering river cuts across a loop and abandons it, leaving the old curved channel isolated from the main flow
A lake formed when a volcanic crater collapses and fills with water
A lake formed purely by wind erosion of a desert surface
explanation: In the mature stage of a river, strong lateral erosion on the outer banks of meanders can eventually cause the river to cut straight across a narrow loop; the abandoned, horseshoe-shaped former channel becomes a stagnant ox-bow lake.

text: Which type of valley is typically formed in the upper (youthful) course of a river?
options: A V-shaped valley
A flat, wide floodplain
A U-shaped valley
A delta
explanation: In the youthful stage, a river flows swiftly down a steep gradient and erodes mainly vertically (downward) into the riverbed, cutting a narrow, steep-sided V-shaped valley.

text: Meandering (large winding curves) in a river's course is most characteristic of its:
options: Delta only, where it finally meets the sea
Very first few metres at its source
Upper (youthful) course, near its source
Middle (mature) course, where the gentler gradient allows lateral erosion to dominate
explanation: As a river enters its middle course, the gradient becomes gentler and vertical erosion decreases, while lateral (sideways) erosion on the outer banks of bends becomes dominant, producing the winding meanders typical of this stage.

text: How are Longitudinal sand dunes formed?
options: They form only along riverbanks, never in open desert
They form entirely underwater, in shallow coastal seas
They always form perpendicular (at right angles) to the wind direction
They form as long ridges running parallel to the direction of a fairly constant, prevailing wind
explanation: Where the wind blows persistently from one direction, sand grains are rolled and piled into long ridges aligned parallel to that wind direction, producing longitudinal (seif) dunes.

text: Barkhan (Barchan) dunes, found in deserts such as the Sahara, are:
options: Crescent-shaped sand dunes formed transverse (at right angles) to the wind direction, with 'horns' pointing downwind
Dunes that form only along riverbanks
Long, straight ridges of sand running parallel to the wind
Dunes made of volcanic ash rather than sand
explanation: Barkhan dunes form where wind blows fairly steadily from one direction over a flat, sandy surface with limited sand supply, producing a crescent shape with the convex side facing the wind and two 'horns' trailing downwind.

text: In which type of region are wind-scooped depressions, known as deflation hollows, most commonly found?
options: Densely populated coastal cities
Equatorial rainforest regions, which have abundant vegetation
Desert regions, where loose, dry and unconsolidated sand is easily picked up and blown away by the wind
Polar regions, which are covered permanently by ice
explanation: In deserts, the lack of vegetation and abundant loose, dry sand allow wind to easily lift and remove (deflate) fine particles from the surface, gradually scooping out shallow depressions called deflation hollows.

text: Why do not all rivers form a delta where they meet the sea?
options: Because deltas only form in cold climates
Because every river without exception eventually forms a delta

Because a delta only forms where the river's sediment load exceeds what tides and sea currents can carry away; rivers entering seas with strong currents or very deep mouths often fail to deposit enough silt
Because delta formation requires volcanic activity nearby
explanation: Delta formation depends on a river depositing more sediment at its mouth than ocean waves, tides and currents can remove; where currents are strong or the coastal shelf drops away steeply, the sediment is swept away before it can accumulate into a delta.

text: A waterfall is typically formed where a river's course crosses:
options: A desert region with sand dunes
The delta at its mouth
A completely flat plain with no change in rock type
A band of hard, resistant rock lying over softer rock, creating a sudden, steep drop as the softer rock erodes faster
explanation: Where a river flows from an area of hard rock onto softer, more easily eroded rock, the softer rock wears away faster, undercutting the hard rock layer and creating a steep step over which the river plunges as a waterfall.

text: Assertion (A): The denudation of the soil cover and its subsequent washing away is described as soil erosion. Reason (R): The process of soil formation and erosion go on simultaneously, and generally there is a balance between the two. Which is correct?
options: A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
Both A and R are true, and R explains A
A is false but R is true
explanation: Both statements are factually correct — soil erosion is indeed the washing away of the soil cover, and soil formation and erosion do normally occur together in balance — but the reason describes a general equilibrium between formation and erosion, not why erosion itself is defined the way it is in the assertion.

text: What are Ocean currents?
options: Random, unpredictable movements of surface water with no fixed pattern
The periodic rise and fall of sea level caused by the Moon's gravity (these are tides)
Large-scale, fairly regular movements of ocean water in a definite direction, driven by factors such as wind, temperature and salinity differences, and the Earth's rotation
Underwater earthquakes that disturb the sea floor
explanation: Ocean currents are large, persistent streams of water that flow through the ocean in fairly predictable paths and directions, influenced mainly by prevailing winds, differences in water temperature and salinity (density), and the Coriolis effect caused by the Earth's rotation.

text: What is a Gyre, in the context of ocean currents?
options: The point where two opposing currents meet and completely cancel out
A particular type of giant ocean wave
A single current that always flows in a straight line
A large circular system of ocean currents, typically formed by the major surface currents within an ocean basin
explanation: A gyre is a large-scale circular pattern of ocean currents, created as surface currents in an ocean basin are deflected by continents and the Coriolis effect, forming a roughly circular flow (e.g. the North Atlantic Gyre).

text: The Gulf Stream is a:
options: Cold ocean current that affects the coast of Japan
Cold ocean current that affects the west coast of South America
Warm ocean current that affects the eastern coast of North America and north-western Europe
Warm ocean current that affects the coast of Australia
explanation: The Gulf Stream is a powerful warm current originating in the Gulf of Mexico that flows north-eastward along the eastern coast of the USA before crossing the Atlantic to warm the coasts of north-western Europe.

text: The Oyashio Current is a:
options: Warm ocean current that affects the coast of Europe
Cold ocean current found off the coast of Africa
Warm ocean current found off the coast of South America
Cold ocean current that flows along the eastern coast of Japan
explanation: The Oyashio is a cold current flowing south from the Arctic region along the eastern coast of Japan, lowering temperatures there compared to the western coast, which is warmed by the Kuroshio Current.

text: The Kuroshio Current, also known as the 'Black Stream', is a:
options: Current found only in the Atlantic Ocean
Cold ocean current that flows along the western coast of Japan
Warm ocean current that flows along the eastern coast of Japan
A tidal current rather than a true ocean current
explanation: The Kuroshio ('Black Stream') is a warm current that flows north-eastward along the eastern coast of Japan, similar in character and effect to the Gulf Stream in the Atlantic.

text: Why do the Grand Banks near Newfoundland form such an important fishing ground of the world?
options: Because it is the warmest patch of water anywhere in the Atlantic Ocean
Because the cold Labrador Current meeting the warm Gulf Stream here causes nutrient-rich upwelling that supports huge populations of plankton and fish
Because of nearby volcanic activity enriching the seawater
Because of unusually heavy monsoon rainfall in the area
explanation: At the Grand Banks, the cold Labrador Current and the warm Gulf Stream converge; this mixing stirs up nutrients from the ocean floor, supporting abundant plankton growth which in turn sustains some of the richest fishing grounds in the world.

text: What is a Tide?
options: A permanent, one-directional ocean current
An underwater earthquake-generated wave
A seasonal change in average sea temperature
The periodic rise and fall of the level of ocean water, caused mainly by the gravitational pull of the Moon and the Sun
explanation: Tides are the regular, periodic rise (high tide) and fall (low tide) of sea level at a given place, produced mainly by the gravitational attraction of the Moon, with a smaller contribution from the Sun.

text: A Spring tide (an unusually high and low tide) occurs when:
options: The Moon is at its farthest point from the Earth in its orbit
The Sun, Earth and Moon are aligned in a straight line (at new moon or full moon), so the gravitational pulls of the Sun and Moon combine
A solar eclipse is taking place
The Sun and Moon are positioned at right angles to each other relative to the Earth
explanation: When the Sun, Earth and Moon line up (at new moon and full moon), the gravitational pulls of the Sun and Moon act together in the same direction, producing unusually high high-tides and unusually low low-tides, called spring tides.

text: A Neap tide (an unusually weak tide, with a smaller difference between high and low tide) occurs when:
options: A lunar eclipse is taking place
The Moon is at its closest point to the Earth in its orbit
The Sun, Earth and Moon are aligned in a straight line
The Sun and Moon are positioned at right angles to each other relative to the Earth, so their gravitational pulls partly cancel each other out
explanation: At first and third quarter moon, the Sun and Moon lie at right angles as seen from Earth, so their gravitational pulls work against each other, reducing the tidal range and producing a neap tide.

text: Why are tides of practical help to fishermen?
options: Tides are of no practical use to fishermen at all
Tides prevent fish from ever entering coastal waters
Tides make the sea surface completely calm at all times
High tide makes it easier and safer for fishing boats to enter and leave harbours, and fish often move closer to shore with the rising tide
explanation: The rise in water level during high tide allows fishing boats to navigate in and out of shallow harbours more safely, and the movement of tidal water often brings fish closer to the shore, making them easier to catch.

chapter: Air (Composition and Structure of the Atmosphere)
text: Which gas has the maximum concentration in the atmosphere of the planet Venus?
options: Carbon dioxide
Oxygen
Nitrogen
Helium
explanation: Venus has a dense atmosphere made up of about 96% carbon dioxide, which traps heat and causes an extreme runaway greenhouse effect on the planet.

chapter: Air (Composition and Structure of the Atmosphere)
text: Which layer of the Earth's atmosphere (up to about 80-90 km) has a fairly uniform proportion of its constituent gases such as nitrogen and oxygen?
options: Homosphere
Exosphere
Ionosphere
Heterosphere
explanation: The homosphere is the lower part of the atmosphere, extending up to about 80-90 km, in which the proportion of major gases like nitrogen and oxygen remains almost constant with height.

chapter: Air (Composition and Structure of the Atmosphere)
text: Which layer of the atmosphere reflects (bounces back) radio waves towards the Earth's surface, aiding long-distance radio communication?
options: Exosphere
Troposphere
Stratosphere
Ionosphere
explanation: The ionosphere contains electrically charged particles (ions) that reflect certain radio wave frequencies back to Earth, which is why it is important for long-distance radio transmission.

chapter: Air (Composition and Structure of the Atmosphere)
text: Which layer of the atmosphere contains the ozone layer that shields the Earth's surface from harmful ultraviolet radiation?
options: Troposphere
Thermosphere
Mesosphere
Stratosphere
explanation: The ozone layer, which absorbs most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet radiation, is located within the stratosphere, roughly 15 to 35 km above the Earth's surface.

chapter: Air (Composition and Structure of the Atmosphere)
text: Why do commercial aircraft generally avoid flying within the troposphere for long stretches when cruising?
options: Because the troposphere contains turbulent weather conditions such as clouds, storms and strong winds that make flight unstable
Because there is no air to breathe at all within the troposphere
Because the troposphere contains no oxygen whatsoever
Because the troposphere is too cold for any aircraft engine to function
explanation: The troposphere is the layer where almost all weather phenomena — clouds, storms, turbulence and strong winds — occur; aircraft usually cruise in the calmer, more stable stratosphere above it whenever practical, to avoid this turbulence.

chapter: Air (Composition and Structure of the Atmosphere)
text: The rare 'mother of pearl' (nacreous) clouds, with their characteristic iridescent colours, are found in which layer of the atmosphere?
options: Stratosphere
Ionosphere
Mesosphere
Troposphere
explanation: Nacreous or 'mother of pearl' clouds form in the lower stratosphere, typically at high latitudes in winter, where extremely cold temperatures allow rare ice crystal clouds to develop well above the normal cloud-forming troposphere.

chapter: Air (Composition and Structure of the Atmosphere)
text: The electrically charged particles (ions) that create the glowing 'Aurora Borealis' display are found mainly in which layer of the atmosphere?
options: Ionosphere
Mesosphere
Stratosphere
Exosphere
explanation: The ionosphere contains ions created when solar radiation and charged particles from the Sun interact with atmospheric gases; near the poles, these charged particles produce the glowing light display known as the Aurora Borealis (Northern Lights).

chapter: Air (Composition and Structure of the Atmosphere)
text: The lower-most boundary of the Stratosphere (separating it from the Troposphere below) is called the:
options: Tropopause
Ionopause
Stratopause
Mesopause
explanation: The tropopause is the transition boundary between the troposphere and the stratosphere; its height varies from about 8 km over the poles to about 18 km over the Equator.

text: What is Insolation?
options: The incoming solar radiation received by the Earth's surface and atmosphere
The temperature of ocean water at a given depth
The pressure exerted by the atmosphere
The heat radiated back outward by the Earth into space
explanation: Insolation (incoming solar radiation) is the solar energy that reaches and is received by a unit area of the Earth's surface in a given time, and is the primary source of heat energy for the Earth-atmosphere system.

text: What is Terrestrial Radiation?
options: The incoming short-wave radiation received directly from the Sun
The energy radiated outward by the Moon
The long-wave heat energy radiated outward by the Earth and its atmosphere, after absorbing incoming solar insolation
The internal heat produced by the Earth's core alone
explanation: After the Earth's surface absorbs short-wave solar insolation, it re-radiates this energy back as long-wave (infrared) terrestrial radiation, which warms the lower atmosphere.

text: The Solar Constant refers to:
options: The total heat radiated by the Earth each year
The fixed surface temperature of the Sun
The average amount of solar energy received at the outer limit of the Earth's atmosphere (about 480 km above sea level)
The constant speed at which sunlight travels
explanation: The solar constant is the average rate at which solar radiation is received just outside the Earth's atmosphere, before any of it is absorbed, reflected or scattered by the atmosphere below.

text: Why does the zone of the Earth lying between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn receive the maximum insolation?
options: Because this zone has no atmosphere above it to absorb sunlight
Because this zone is physically closest to the Sun
Because this zone has the least cloud cover of anywhere on Earth
Because the Sun's rays strike this zone almost vertically throughout the year, concentrating more energy over a smaller surface area
explanation: Within the tropics, the Sun's rays fall at a high angle (close to vertical) for most of the year, so the same amount of solar energy is concentrated over a smaller area, producing more intense heating than at higher latitudes where rays strike obliquely.

text: Why do areas closer to the sea generally have a lower daily and annual range of temperature than interior (continental) areas?
options: Because of the speed of the Earth's rotation near coastlines
Because water heats up and cools down much more slowly than land, moderating coastal temperatures (an equable, maritime climate)
Because the sea completely blocks all sunlight from reaching the coast
Because coastal areas receive far less insolation than inland areas
explanation: Water has a higher specific heat capacity than land, so seas and oceans warm up and cool down far more gradually; this moderating maritime influence keeps nearby coastal regions from experiencing the large temperature swings seen in continental interiors.

text: What is a Temperature Inversion?
options: A permanent feature of climate found only exactly at the Equator
The usual, normal decrease of temperature with increasing altitude
A sudden, unexpected drop in daytime temperature
A reversal of the normal pattern, where temperature increases with height instead of decreasing, often occurring on clear, calm nights
explanation: Normally temperature falls with height (the normal lapse rate); in an inversion, the ground cools rapidly on a clear, calm night and becomes colder than the air just above it, so temperature actually rises with height near the surface.

text: How does global warming lead to a radiation imbalance in the Earth's atmosphere?
options: Because the Sun is producing noticeably less energy than it used to
Because volcanic ash now permanently blocks all incoming sunlight
Because the Earth has physically moved farther away from the Sun
Increased greenhouse gases trap more outgoing long-wave terrestrial radiation than is naturally released into space, so more heat is retained than escapes
explanation: Greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide and methane absorb and re-radiate outgoing terrestrial (long-wave) radiation; as their concentration rises, more heat is trapped within the Earth-atmosphere system than is lost to space, upsetting the natural balance and raising global temperatures.

text: What is Atmospheric pressure?
options: The temperature of the air at a given place
The amount of water vapour present in the air
The speed at which wind blows at a given location
The force (weight) exerted by a column of air on a given unit area of the Earth's surface
explanation: Atmospheric pressure is the force exerted per unit area by the weight of the column of air above that point, and it decreases with increasing altitude as there is progressively less air above.

text: Why does atmospheric pressure decrease as altitude increases?
options: Because temperature always increases steadily with altitude
Because the proportion of oxygen increases with altitude
Because gravity becomes stronger at higher altitudes
Because both the density of air and the weight of the overlying column of air decrease with height
explanation: As one moves upward, there is progressively less air remaining above to exert weight, and the air itself becomes less dense; both factors cause atmospheric pressure to fall steadily with increasing altitude.

text: What is a Jet Stream?
options: A type of strong, warm ocean current
A type of ocean tide
A strong wind that blows only over deserts
A narrow band of very fast-moving, high-altitude winds found near the top of the troposphere
explanation: Jet streams are narrow, fast-flowing ribbons of air found at high altitudes (near the tropopause), blowing from west to east, and are used by pilots to save fuel and time when flying in the same direction as the stream.

text: Which of the following is an example of a Permanent (Planetary) wind, as opposed to a periodic or local wind?
options: The Trade Winds, which blow consistently from the sub-tropical high-pressure belts towards the equatorial low-pressure belt
The seasonal monsoon winds of South Asia
The Loo, a hot seasonal wind of northern India
Local land and sea breezes
explanation: Permanent (planetary) winds, like the Trade Winds and Westerlies, blow steadily throughout the year in a fixed general direction because of the Earth's permanent global pressure belts, unlike periodic winds (monsoons) or local winds (land/sea breezes) which change with the season or time of day.

text: Why are the Westerlies also known as Anti-trade winds?
options: Because they blow only at and around the Equator
Because they blow in roughly the opposite direction to the Trade Winds, moving from the sub-tropical high-pressure belt towards the sub-polar low-pressure belt
Because they blow only over the open ocean, never over land
Because they are the coldest permanent winds found anywhere on Earth
explanation: While the Trade Winds blow from the sub-tropical high towards the equatorial low, the Westerlies blow from the same sub-tropical high-pressure belt but in the opposite direction, towards the sub-polar low — hence the name Anti-trade winds.

text: Why do the Westerlies in the Southern Hemisphere blow with much greater force and consistency than those in the Northern Hemisphere?
options: Because gravity is slightly stronger in the Southern Hemisphere
Because the Southern Hemisphere has many more mountain ranges blocking local winds
Because the Southern Hemisphere is physically closer to the Sun
Because the Southern Hemisphere has a much larger expanse of open ocean with far fewer landmasses to obstruct the wind's flow
explanation: The Southern Hemisphere is covered mostly by unbroken ocean at the latitudes where the Westerlies blow, offering little frictional resistance from land; this allows them to blow with far greater strength and regularity than in the Northern Hemisphere, where more landmasses interrupt the flow.

text: What is the other, more common, name for the Sub-Tropical High-Pressure belt?
options: Horse Latitudes
Doldrums
Furious Fifties
Roaring Forties
explanation: The Sub-Tropical High-Pressure belts, located around 30 degrees N and S, are also known as the Horse Latitudes, a name traditionally linked to sailing ships becoming stranded there in calm winds.

text: Why is the Sub-Tropical High-Pressure belt known as a 'belt of divergence'?
options: Because winds from all directions converge together here
Because air descends here and then spreads outward (diverges) towards both the Equator and the poles
Because it is the belt with the very lowest pressure found on Earth
Because it marks a point where the Earth's magnetic field diverges
explanation: In the sub-tropical high-pressure belt, air that has risen at the Equator descends back towards the surface; upon reaching the ground it spreads out (diverges) both equatorward (as the Trade Winds) and poleward (as the Westerlies).

text: Anti-cyclones are generally associated with:
options: Violent, destructive tornadoes
Heavy storms and intense rainfall
Fine, calm and generally clear weather
Sudden volcanic eruptions
explanation: In an anti-cyclone, air descends from above and diverges outward near the surface; this descending, subsiding air inhibits cloud formation, generally producing calm, dry and clear weather, unlike the stormy conditions associated with cyclones.

text: What is the Coriolis force, and how does it affect moving winds?
options: It is a force caused entirely by mountains blocking the flow of wind
It is an apparent deflective force, caused by the Earth's rotation, that bends moving winds to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere
It is a real force that acts only on ocean currents, not on winds
It is a force that acts only exactly at the Equator
explanation: Because the Earth rotates, any object or fluid moving across its surface (including wind) appears to be deflected from its straight-line path — to the right of its direction of motion in the Northern Hemisphere, and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere; this is known as the Coriolis effect.

text: What is Humidity?
options: The speed at which wind blows
The temperature of the air
The pressure exerted by the air
The amount of water vapour present in the air
explanation: Humidity refers to the moisture content, or the amount of water vapour, present in the atmosphere at a given place and time.

text: How does Relative Humidity differ from Absolute Humidity?
options: They are exactly the same measurement, just with different names
Absolute humidity is always greater in value than relative humidity

Relative humidity is the percentage of water vapour present compared to the maximum the air could hold at that temperature, while absolute humidity is the actual mass of water vapour present per unit volume of air
Relative humidity has no relationship with air temperature at all
explanation: Absolute humidity is the actual quantity of water vapour contained in a given volume of air, whereas relative humidity expresses this as a percentage of the maximum amount of vapour the air could hold at its current temperature before becoming saturated.

text: The Dew Point is defined as:
options: The surface temperature of the Earth recorded at noon
The average daily temperature of a place
The temperature at which water freezes into ice
The temperature at which air becomes fully saturated with water vapour and condensation begins
explanation: When air is cooled to its dew point, it can no longer hold all the water vapour it contains, so the excess vapour begins to condense into tiny water droplets, forming dew, fog or cloud.

text: Convectional rainfall is characterised by:
options: Intense localised surface heating causing moist air to rise rapidly, cool and condense, producing heavy but short-duration showers, typically in the afternoon
A long, gentle and widespread drizzle lasting many hours
Rain caused only by air being forced to rise over a mountain barrier
Rain that occurs exclusively at night, never during the day
explanation: Convectional rainfall occurs when the ground is heated strongly (common in equatorial and tropical regions), causing warm, moist air to rise quickly, cool, and condense into towering cumulonimbus clouds that release intense, short-lived showers, often in the late afternoon.

text: Orographic (relief) rainfall occurs when:
options: Winds blow only over open water, far from any landmass
Moist winds are forced to rise over a mountain barrier, cool and condense, giving heavy rain on the windward side and comparatively little on the leeward (rain shadow) side
Air rises purely due to intense localised surface heating, with no mountain involved
Warm and cold air masses meet along a front
explanation: When moisture-laden winds encounter a mountain range, they are forced upward along the windward slope; as they rise and cool, the moisture condenses and falls as rain, while the leeward slope receives little rainfall as the now-dry air descends and warms.

text: Why do the windward slopes of a mountain receive much more rainfall than the leeward slopes?
options: Because moist winds rise and cool on the windward side, releasing their moisture there, while the air descending on the leeward side is already dry and warming, creating a 'rain shadow'
Because leeward slopes are always at a higher altitude than windward slopes
Because windward slopes always face directly towards the Equator
Because leeward slopes receive no wind of any kind
explanation: As moist air is forced up the windward slope, it cools and releases most of its moisture as rain; by the time the now much drier air crosses the summit and descends the leeward slope, it warms and holds what little moisture remains, producing a dry 'rain shadow' area.

text: Frontal (cyclonic) rainfall occurs along the:
options: Boundary zone, called a front, where warm and cold air masses meet, forcing the lighter warm air to rise and condense
Equatorial belt alone, with no connection to air masses
Polar ice caps alone
Windward side of a mountain range only
explanation: A front is the boundary where a warm air mass meets a cooler, denser air mass; the warm air is forced to rise over the cooler air, cooling and condensing as it does so, producing frontal (cyclonic) rainfall, which is common in the mid-latitudes.

text: Why is cyclonic rainfall also sometimes called 'Frontal rainfall'?
options: Because it occurs where a travelling depression or cyclone brings warm and cold air masses together along a front, forcing the warmer air to rise and release rain
Because it only occurs at the North Pole
Because it has no connection whatsoever to air masses
Because it is caused by nearby volcanic eruptions
explanation: Temperate cyclones form at the boundary (front) between warm tropical and cold polar air masses; as the cyclone moves, it brings this frontal boundary with it, so the rainfall it produces is called both cyclonic and frontal rainfall.

text: The dark, funnel-shaped cloud that extends downward from the base of a severe thunderstorm, associated with violently rotating winds, is called a:
options: Anticyclone
Cirrus cloud
Nimbostratus cloud
Tornado
explanation: A tornado is a violently rotating column of air, visibly extending as a dark funnel cloud from the base of a severe thunderstorm down towards the ground, capable of causing extreme, concentrated destruction.

text: What is a Pollutant?
options: Any valuable mineral found within a rock
Any form of renewable energy
Any natural gas that is normally present in clean air
Any substance introduced into the environment that has an undesirable or harmful effect on living organisms
explanation: A pollutant is any harmful substance or energy (solid, liquid, gas, noise, etc.) that, when introduced into air, water or soil, causes adverse or undesirable effects on living organisms and the environment.

text: Which of the following is an example of a biodegradable pollutant?
options: Plastic bottles
Domestic kitchen and food waste
Heavy metal industrial waste
Glass bottles
explanation: Biodegradable pollutants, such as kitchen scraps and other organic waste, can be broken down naturally by microorganisms over a relatively short time, unlike non-biodegradable materials such as plastic, glass or heavy metals.

text: Why are non-biodegradable pollutants considered particularly harmful to the environment?
options: Because they affect only plants and have no impact on animals
Because they always produce a strong, unpleasant smell
Because they dissolve completely and harmlessly in water
Because they do not break down naturally and persist in the environment for a very long time, accumulating and causing long-term damage
explanation: Non-biodegradable pollutants such as plastics and certain chemicals cannot be broken down by natural microbial processes, so they accumulate over decades or longer in soil, water and even within the bodies of living organisms, causing persistent harm.

text: How do primary pollutants differ from secondary pollutants?
options: Primary pollutants occur only in water, never in air
They are exactly the same type of pollutant, with no real difference

Primary pollutants are released directly into the environment from a source (e.g. vehicle exhaust), while secondary pollutants form later through chemical reactions involving primary pollutants in the atmosphere (e.g. smog)
Secondary pollutants are always far less harmful than primary pollutants
explanation: A primary pollutant, such as carbon monoxide from a vehicle's exhaust, is emitted directly from its source, while a secondary pollutant, such as the ozone found in photochemical smog, is formed afterwards by chemical reactions between primary pollutants and sunlight or other atmospheric gases.

text: Why are nuclear radiations considered more dangerous than many other forms of pollution?
options: Because nuclear radiation is always clearly visible to the naked eye
Because nuclear waste always has a strong, noticeable smell
Because nuclear radiation affects only marine animals, not humans
Because radioactive contamination can cause severe, long-term genetic damage and cancer, and can persist and spread its effects across generations
explanation: Unlike many other pollutants whose effects are immediate and localised, radioactive contamination can cause invisible but severe damage to living cells and DNA, leading to cancers and genetic mutations that can affect not just the exposed individual but also future generations.
